extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in political economy and public finance
extracted.subtask_description: A normative and analytical treatment of different kinds of taxes (poll/capitation, transfer/inheritance, stamp/registration, wages, consumption) and their economic incidence, equity, administrative effects, and consequences for capital and productive labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes on transference diminish capital value
rubrics_metrics.description: While property remains in the possession of the same person, permanent taxes are intended to take away some part of the revenue only; but when property changes hands (from the dead to the living, or from the living to the living) such taxes have frequently been imposed upon it as necessarily take away some part of its capital value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the Roman vicesima hereditatum (twentieth penny on successions), Dutch succession duties, and feudal casualties and reliefs. These taxes reduce the capital transmitted and therefore the funds available for productive labour; they are often levied directly on public/notorious transfers (inheritances, land transfers) and indirectly (stamps, registration) on movable transfers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stamp duties and registration as indirect taxation of transfers
rubrics_metrics.description: Transference of movable property is often taxed indirectly by requiring deeds to be written on stamped paper or to be recorded in a register, under penalty of invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two chief modes: (1) stamped paper/parchment (stamp duty), (2) recording/registration duties. Examples and contrasts given for England, Holland, and France (variation in proportionality, price of stamps, registration duties percentage like 2.5% in Holland). Administrative design (which deeds must be stamped/registered) affects equity and incidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incidence of taxes on sales and transfers of land and houses
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxes upon the sale of land fall altogether upon the seller (the seller is almost always under the necessity of selling), whereas taxes upon the sale of new-built houses, where building is sold without the ground, fall generally upon the buyer (the builder must get his profit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether burden falls on seller or buyer depends on market necessities and demand. Taxes on sale therefore frequently fall on necessitous persons and can be 'cruel and oppressive.' Ground-rents and mortgages sale taxes fall on sellers for same reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes upon the profits of stock can affect interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxes upon the profits of stock, in particular employments, can affect the interest of money; taxes upon the revenue arising from stock in all employments, where levied with exactness, will in many cases fall upon the interest of money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the French vingtieme (twentieth penny) is assessed on revenues of land, houses, and stock and, so far as it affects stock and is exactly levied, may fall altogether upon the interest of money. The exactness of assessment matters to incidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct taxes on wages: incidence and distortion
rubrics_metrics.description: A direct tax upon the wages of labour cannot properly be said to be advanced by the labourer in the long-run; wages will rise by more than the proportion of the tax, and the person who immediately employs labour will in reality advance the tax (with something more).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: with ordinary wages of 10s and a tax of one-fifth, wages must rise to 12s6d so the labourer nets 10s after tax; employers (manufacturers, farmers) advance the rise and pass it on as higher prices or lower rents, so final payment falls upon consumers, landlords, or both. Direct wage taxes also tend to reduce demand for labour and the annual produce of land and labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes intended to fall indifferently: capitation and consumption taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxes intended to fall indifferently upon every species of revenue are capitation (poll) taxes and taxes upon consumable commodities; they must be paid out of whatever revenue the contributor possesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitation taxes and consumption taxes are used when revenue cannot be assessed proportionally. Their practical effects and equity depend on design: capitation taxes face tradeoffs between equality and certainty; consumption taxes depend heavily on whether taxed goods are necessaries or luxuries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitation (poll) taxes: certainty vs. equality tradeoff
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitation taxes, if attempted to be proportioned to fortune, become altogether arbitrary; if proportioned by rank, they become altogether unequal. Attempting equality makes them arbitrary and uncertain; attempting certainty makes them unequal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: English poll-taxes rated many by rank; French capitation combined rank-based tariffs for higher orders and fortune-based assessments for lower orders, with intendants tasked to raise fixed sums. Capitation taxes are cheap to levy and, where rigorously exacted, yield sure revenue, but are often regressive and arbitrary for the poor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumption taxes: distinction between necessaries and luxuries
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumable commodities are either necessaries or luxuries. Necessaries are those the custom of the country renders indecent for creditable people to be without; all other things are luxuries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taxes on necessaries operate like direct taxes on wages (they raise prices of necessities and thus wages must rise to allow labourers to purchase subsistence), whereas taxes on luxuries are less likely to burden the poor. Examples: linen shirts and leather shoes considered necessaries in Britain; beer/ale and wine treated as luxuries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stamp duties have multiple natures (transfer vs consumption)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some stamp duties (cards, dice, newspapers, periodicals) are properly taxes upon consumption; others (stamps on deeds, licences) are taxes upon transference or on privileges but are levied by the same officers and in the same manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although called by the same name and collected similarly, stamp duties fall on different funds depending on the object taxed: consumable-item stamps fall on consumers; licence stamps intended to fall on retailers are often finally paid by consumers as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration of immoveable-property rights is socially useful; secret registers and revenue-motivated proliferation harmful
rubrics_metrics.description: The registration of mortgages and of rights upon immoveable property gives great security to creditors and purchasers and is advantageous to the public; registers which ought to be kept secret ought never to exist and the credit of individuals should not depend on the probity of inferior officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When registration fees become a source of sovereign revenue, register-offices multiply (often unnecessarily) and secret registers proliferate, producing abuses. Registration systems should be limited to what benefits public security and not used merely to extract revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transference taxes are 'unthrifty'—they increase sovereign revenue but reduce productive capital
rubrics_metrics.description: All taxes upon the transference of property of every kind, so far as they diminish the capital value of that property, tend to diminish the funds destined for the maintenance of productive labour. They are more or less unthrifty taxes that increase the revenue of the sovereign, which seldom maintains any but unproductive labourers, at the expense of the capital of the people, which maintains none but productive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers should be aware that levying revenue via transference taxes reallocates capital from productive uses to support of the sovereign's (often unproductive) expenditures. Even when proportional to transfer value, such taxes are unequal because frequency of transfer differs among assets of equal value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and certainty in tax law to prevent abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Uncertainty in the words of edicts or laws which impose taxes gives occasion to extortion and arbitrary collection; many complaints against registration duties (the Controle) in France arose from such imprecision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tax rules should be precise and distinct to avoid discretionary abuse by collectors; lack of precision—not the tax's nature—is often responsible for arbitrary and uncertain exactions.
